s: Mitakshara is a commentary on which of the following texts?
x: Mitakshara is a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, composed by Vijnaneshwara.
tq: Directly identify the foundational text associated with a major legal work.
sec: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

s:
With reference to the Mitakshara and Dayabhaga schools, consider the following statements:
1. Under Mitakshara, sons acquire a right in ancestral property by birth.
2. Under Dayabhaga, sons acquire such a right only after the death of the father.
3. Dayabhaga was principally followed in Bengal and Assam.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Mitakshara recognises the sons’ right by birth, whereas Dayabhaga postpones it until the father’s death and was followed mainly in Bengal and Assam.
tq: Split the options by testing each row of the comparison separately.
sec: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

s: Which one of the following regions was NOT associated with a Mitakshara sub-school or its principal area of application?
x: Bengal was associated with the Dayabhaga school. Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra and Dravida were associated with Mitakshara traditions or sub-schools.
tq: Find the region belonging to the confusable rival school.
sec: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

s: Which one of the following statements correctly distinguishes Mitakshara from Dayabhaga?
o: Mitakshara deals with criminal law, whereas Dayabhaga deals with civil law.
Mitakshara gives sons a right in ancestral property by birth, whereas Dayabhaga recognises it after the father’s death.
Mitakshara applied only to upper castes, whereas Dayabhaga applied only to lower castes.
Mitakshara was confined to Bengal, whereas Dayabhaga prevailed throughout India.
x: The principal distinction is that Mitakshara recognises the sons’ right in ancestral property by birth, while Dayabhaga recognises it only after the father’s death. The caste-based distinction is incorrect.
tq: Discriminate between two similar legal schools by their precise inheritance rule.
sec: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Vijnaneshwara — Mitakshara
2. Hemadri — Chaturvarga Chintamani
3. Jimutavahana — Dayabhaga
4. Rajasekhara — Medieval jurist
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Rajasekhara was a poet-dramatist, not a jurist.
tq: Use the wrong-person-for-the-work trap to eliminate the mismatched pair.
sec: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

s: The Hindu Succession Act rests largely on the legal principles of which of the following?
x: The Hindu Succession Act still rests largely on the principles of the Mitakshara school.
tq: Link a historical legal school with its continuing legal significance.
sec: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

s: Who among the following overthrew the last Rashtrakuta ruler Karka II in 973 CE?
x: Tailapa II overthrew the last Rashtrakuta ruler, Karka II, in 973 CE and founded the Kalyani Chalukya line.
tq: Match the ruler with the specific overthrow and foundation event.

s:
Arrange the following rulers in chronological order of their reign or political prominence:
A. Tailapa II
B. Satyasraya
C. Someshvara I
D. Vikramaditya VI
x: Tailapa II preceded Satyasraya; Someshvara I followed Satyasraya, and Vikramaditya VI came later.
tq: Fix the earliest founder first and then place the successive rulers.

s: Satyasraya’s expedition against Vengi under Bayyalanambi in 1006 CE was repulsed by:
x: Satyasraya sent Bayyalanambi against Vengi in 1006 CE, but Saktivarman I, aided by the Cholas, repulsed the expedition.
tq: Use the commander–opponent–ally relationship rather than the date alone.

s: Which ruler backed Vijayaditya VII against Rajaraja Narendra?
x: Jayasimha II supported Vijayaditya VII in opposition to Rajaraja Narendra.
tq: Identify the ruler from the claimant he supported.

s:
Someshvara I is associated with which of the following sets of achievements?
1. Killing Rajadhiraja I at Koppam
2. Assuming the title Vengi Purveshwara
3. Granting Hanamkonda to Kakatiya Prola I
4. Founding the Chalukya-Vikrama era
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: Someshvara I killed Rajadhiraja I at Koppam, assumed the title Vengi Purveshwara and granted Hanamkonda to Prola I. The Chalukya-Vikrama era was founded by Vikramaditya VI.
tq: Separate achievements of closely related rulers by checking the founder claim.

s: Someshvara I, also known as Ahavamalla, ruled during which period?
x: Someshvara I Ahavamalla ruled from 1042 to 1068 CE.
tq: Use the reign-period figures to distinguish successive rulers.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes Vikramaditya VI?
o: He ruled for 12 years and founded the Kalyani Chalukya dynasty.
He was defeated by Someshvara I at Kudalasangamam.
He was the author of Manasollasa and ruled from 1126 to 1138 CE.
He ruled for 50 years, assumed the title Tribhuvanamalla and brought Vengi feudatories under his control.
x: Vikramaditya VI was the greatest Kalyani Chalukya ruler, ruled for 50 years, bore the title Tribhuvanamalla and brought the Vengi feudatories under his authority.
tq: Combine the ruler’s title, duration and major achievement to identify the correct option.

s: Vikramaditya VI ruled from:
x: Vikramaditya VI ruled from 1076 to 1126 CE.
tq: Test the exact reign period using closely spaced historical dates.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Someshvara III — Koppam victory over Rajadhiraja I
x: Vikramaditya VI assumed the title Tribhuvanamalla. The other achievements belong to different rulers.
tq: Detect the swapped ruler-and-achievement combinations.

s: The capital of the Kalyani Chalukyas was:
x: Kalyani, now known as Basavakalyan in Karnataka, was the capital of the Kalyani Chalukyas.
tq: Distinguish the capital of one Chalukya branch from those of other branches and successor powers.

s: The Chalukya-Vikrama era was:
o: started by Someshvara III in 1126 CE to commemorate Manasollasa
founded by Tailapa II in 973 CE after defeating the Rashtrakutas
introduced by Someshvara I after the battle of Koppam in 1053 CE
founded by Vikramaditya VI in 1076 CE and used in place of the Saka era in royal records
x: Vikramaditya VI founded the Chalukya-Vikrama era in 1076 CE, the year of his accession, replacing the Saka era in royal records.
tq: Match the era with its founder, starting year and administrative use.

s: Bilhana, the author of Vikramankadevacharita, was originally from:
x: Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet who served at the court of Vikramaditya VI.
tq: Identify the author through his place of origin and court association.
sec: Bilhana - origin, patron, subject of his work

s: Vikramankadevacharita is best described as:
o: a legal commentary on inheritance law
an encyclopaedia of South Indian cuisine
a historical mahakavya on Vikramaditya VI’s life and conquests
x: Bilhana’s Vikramankadevacharita is a historical mahakavya dealing with the life and conquests of Vikramaditya VI.
tq: Distinguish literary genre and subject from other works in the same period.
sec: Bilhana - origin, patron, subject of his work

s: According to Bilhana’s account, the Chalukyas originated at:
x: Bilhana claimed that the Chalukyas originated at a place called Brahmachulakam.
tq: Recall the distinctive origin-place mentioned by the court poet.
sec: Bilhana - origin, patron, subject of his work

s: Which one of the following statements about Bilhana is correct?
o: He was a Bengal jurist who wrote the Dayabhaga.
He was a Kashmiri poet at Vikramaditya VI’s court and compared the ruler’s reign with Ramarajya.
He was a Virashaiva saint who composed Vachana literature.
He was a Yadava minister who wrote Chaturvarga Chintamani.
x: Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet at Vikramaditya VI’s court and likened the ruler’s reign to Ramarajya. The other descriptions refer to different persons or traditions.
tq: Apply the wrong-author-for-the-work and wrong-origin traps.
sec: Bilhana - origin, patron, subject of his work

s: Manasollasa, also known as Abhilashitartha Chintamani, was composed by:
x: Someshvara III, who ruled from 1126 to 1138 CE, was the author of Manasollasa or Abhilashitartha Chintamani.
tq: Match the literary work with the correct ruler-author.

s:
Which of the following subjects are dealt with in Manasollasa?
1. Statecraft
2. Agriculture
3. Medicine and astronomy
4. Music, dance and cuisine
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: Manasollasa is a 100-chapter Sanskrit encyclopaedia covering all the listed subjects, including statecraft, agriculture, medicine, astronomy, music, dance and cuisine.
tq: Treat an encyclopaedic work as a multi-subject list and test every component.

s: Manasollasa is regarded as an important early record of:
x: Manasollasa is regarded as the earliest major record of South Indian recipes.
tq: Identify the distinctive cultural contribution of the encyclopaedia.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Vikramankadevacharita was written by Bilhana. Nagavarma II wrote Kavyavalokana and Karnataka Bhashabhushana, while Basavanna was associated with Virashaiva Vachana literature.
tq: Find the author-work mismatch among nearby literary personalities.

s: The principal cause of the Chola–Chalukya wars was:
o: control of Vengi and the struggle for supremacy in the Deccan
competition over the port of Kolhapur alone
a religious conflict between Shaivism and Buddhism
a dispute over the succession to the Rashtrakuta throne alone
x: The wars arose mainly from succession disputes in Vengi, with each side backing a claimant, and from the wider struggle for supremacy in the Deccan.
tq: Separate the immediate succession issue from the broader political objective.

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kalidindi — Rajendra I defeated the Kalyani forces and Vijayaditya VII
2. Dharanikota — Rajadhiraja I defeated Vijayaditya VII and burned Kollipaka
3. Koppam — Someshvara I killed Rajadhiraja I
4. Kudalasangamam — Virarajendra defeated Someshvara I
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The battles record alternating Chola and Kalyani Chalukya successes in the contest over Vengi and Deccan supremacy.
tq: Start from the sure battle-result pairs and verify each pairing.

s: At the battle of Koppam in 1053 CE, which event occurred?
o: Virarajendra defeated Someshvara I and installed Vijayaditya VII.
Rajendra I defeated Vijayaditya VII at Kalidindi.
Rajadhiraja I killed Someshvara I and captured Kalyani.
Someshvara I killed Rajadhiraja I, while Rajendra II was crowned on the battlefield and claimed victory.
x: At Koppam, Someshvara I killed the Chola ruler Rajadhiraja I. Rajendra II was then crowned on the field and claimed victory.
tq: Use the battlefield succession event to distinguish Koppam from the other battles.

s: The battle of Kudalasangamam, fought around 1062 CE, ended with:
o: the defeat of Virarajendra by Someshvara I
the defeat of Rajendra II by Satyasraya
the defeat of Someshvara I by Virarajendra
the defeat of Rajadhiraja I by Vijayaditya VII
x: At Kudalasangamam, approximately in 1062 CE, the Chola ruler Virarajendra defeated Someshvara I.
tq: Combine the approximate date with the correct victor and defeated ruler.

s: Rajendra II set up a victory pillar at:
x: Rajendra II established a victory pillar at Kolhapur after the Chola–Chalukya conflict.
tq: Distinguish the commemorative site from the battlefield names.

s: Which statement regarding Takkolam is correct?
o: It was the site where Rajendra II was crowned in 1053 CE.
It was a battle between Vikramaditya VI and the Hoysalas in 1076 CE.
It was a battle of the Kalyani Chalukyas against the Yadavas in 1156 CE.
It was fought in 949 CE between Rashtrakuta Krishna III and the Cholas.
x: Takkolam was fought in 949 CE between Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna III and the Cholas; it was not a Kalyani Chalukya–Chola battle.
tq: Separate a frequently confused earlier Rashtrakuta–Chola battle from the Kalyani conflicts.

s: The mature architectural style of the Kalyani Chalukyas is generally known as:
o: Dravida style of the Pallavas alone
x: Kalyani Chalukya architecture is associated with the mature Vesara, also called the Gadag style.
tq: Identify the architectural style from the dynasty-style association.
sec: Kalyani Chalukya art - Lakkundi, Itagi Mahadeva temple

s:
Which of the following features is associated with Kalyani Chalukya temple architecture?
1. Use of chloritic schist or soapstone
2. Stellate plans
3. Influence on later Hoysala architecture
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: Kalyani Chalukya temples used chloritic schist or soapstone, often employed star-shaped plans, and provided a model for later Hoysala architecture.
tq: Test material, plan and later influence as three separate architectural clues.
sec: Kalyani Chalukya art - Lakkundi, Itagi Mahadeva temple

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Mahadeva Temple is at Itagi. Kasivishveshvara is at Lakkundi, Doddabasappa is at Dambal and Kedareshwara is at Balligavi.
tq: Use the temple–location pair as the sure pair and eliminate the swapped locations.
sec: Kalyani Chalukya art - Lakkundi, Itagi Mahadeva temple

s: The Itagi Mahadeva temple is popularly described as the:
x: The Itagi Mahadeva temple is popularly known as the “Emperor among temples.”
tq: Recall the distinctive epithet attached to the monument.
sec: Kalyani Chalukya art - Lakkundi, Itagi Mahadeva temple

s:
Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
1. Kasivishveshvara — Lakkundi
2. Doddabasappa — Dambal
3. Kedareshwara — Balligavi
4. Mahadeva — Lakkundi
x: The Mahadeva temple is at Itagi, not Lakkundi. Kasivishveshvara, Doddabasappa and Kedareshwara are correctly associated with Lakkundi, Dambal and Balligavi respectively.
tq: Find the single location swap in a list of closely related monuments.
sec: Kalyani Chalukya art - Lakkundi, Itagi Mahadeva temple

s: Which successor power was centred at Dwarasamudra in southern Karnataka?
x: The Hoysalas were based in southern Karnataka, with Dwarasamudra as their capital.
tq: Match each successor power with its regional capital.

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Hoysalas — Dwarasamudra
2. Yadavas or Seunas — Devagiri
3. Kakatiyas — Hanamkonda–Warangal
4. Kalachuris — Kalyani
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correct. These powers emerged in different regions after the weakening of Kalyani Chalukya authority.
tq: Start from the capital pairs and confirm that no region has been shifted between successor powers.

s: Who seized the throne at Kalyani around 1156 CE?
x: Kalachuri ruler Bijjala seized the throne at Kalyani around 1156 CE.
tq: Match the seizure of the central throne with the correct successor power.

s:
Which of the following statements about the end of Kalyani Chalukya authority is correct?
1. The dynasty ended around 1189 CE.
2. Kalyani and Hoysala attacks helped end the Chalukya–Chola hold over Vengi.
3. The Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and Yadavas emerged as important successor powers.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: All three statements are correct. The dynasty ended around 1189 CE, while successor powers expanded and the Chalukya–Chola hold over Vengi weakened.
tq: Combine the date of decline with the regional consequences of political fragmentation.

s: The Kalyani Chalukyas were significant in Indian history because they:
o: abolished hereditary rights in ancestral property
checked Chola expansion northwards and contributed to the development of Hindu legal tradition through Mitakshara
unified all of northern India under one empire
ended the Gupta Empire and introduced Persian administration
x: The Kalyani Chalukyas checked Chola expansion towards the north, while the Mitakshara tradition associated with their court shaped Hindu inheritance law for about a millennium.
tq: Select the option combining the dynasty’s political and legal significance without an unrelated claim.

s: Which statement best explains the importance of Vengi in Chola–Chalukya relations?
o: Vengi was permanently outside the political interests of both powers.
Vengi was important only as the birthplace of Bilhana.
Vengi was the principal prize because succession disputes there enabled both powers to support rival claimants.
Vengi was the capital of the Yadavas in Maharashtra.
x: Vengi was the central arena of succession disputes, and both the Cholas and Kalyani Chalukyas backed rival claimants to gain political control.
tq: Apply the cause of the wars to a political succession scenario.

s: According to the Khazipet inscription, the Kakatiyas’ early rise was connected with:
o: the conquest of Devagiri from the Yadavas
the founding of Dwarasamudra by the Hoysalas
the seizure of Kalyani by Bijjala
a grant of Hanamkonda with hereditary rights
x: The Khazipet inscription records Hanamkonda being granted with hereditary rights, reflecting the Kakatiyas’ rise as feudatories.
tq: Use an inscriptional clue to identify the political basis of a dynasty’s rise.

s:
Which of the following correctly compares the three major Chalukya branches?
1. Badami Chalukyas — Vatapi — sixth to eighth centuries
2. Kalyani Chalukyas — late tenth to twelfth centuries
3. Vengi Chalukyas — seventh to eleventh centuries
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: All three comparisons are correct. Badami, Kalyani and Vengi represent distinct Chalukya branches belonging to different periods and centres.
tq: Compare dynasty, centre and period together to avoid confusing distinct Chalukya branches.

s: Which one of the following sequences correctly arranges the three Chalukya branches from the earliest to the latest broad period?
x: The broad periods are Badami from the sixth to eighth centuries, Vengi from the seventh to eleventh centuries, and Kalyani from the late tenth to twelfth centuries.
tq: Arrange overlapping dynastic periods by their earliest starting point and broad duration.
